prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B033 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange tested the case for three things, and it held on each. The mechanism is stable, since incretin physiology, proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of the truncated peptide explain why degradation-resistant agonists work. The clinical effect has been confirmed by independent trials on glycaemia, weight and cardiorenal outcomes. The discovery can be stated in one sentence. All six of us converged on the same trio, but I treat that as a reason to look harder at the third slot, not as evidence. Holst and Drucker are secure on any reading of the record: Holst for secretion and incretin action in humans, Drucker for receptor biology, the intestinotropic and metabolic actions and the therapeutic rationale. I keep Mojsov for the active GLP-1(7-36) form, which is the step that turned a proglucagon fragment into a hormone with a defined action. I keep the citation on the physiology and the active form and let its closing clause show the therapeutic consequence. That reaches the medicine without adding a fourth name.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still the third slot and the missing names. I cannot verify the priority record for the active peptide from the supplied files. Habener, and Bell as Perlmann notes, are outside the credit list, and I cannot say how their work should move the allocation. Knudsen is left out by the cap, so the prize honours the physiology and not the long-acting analogues patients take. If the committee were to find that Mojsov's priority cannot be defended, my fallback would be to test a Holst and Drucker pair, and I would not fill the vacated slot automatically. If it decided the prize must reach the drugs, I would want that debated as a deliberate change of principle. A discovery-only prize can be defended, but it is not free of criticism. I am also not convinced that a second part is warranted this year. B039 is my first alternative, but its credit list lacks Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept.

responses.point: Marie Wahren-Herlenius holds that Holst and Drucker are secure under any resolution of the priority question. She names Knudsen as the strongest replacement if Mojsov cannot be defended, and says that if the drugs are to be recognised it should be as a separate part or in a different year.
responses.response: I agree that Holst and Drucker cannot be removed on principle. I also agree that if Mojsov falls, Knudsen is the most natural substitute under the cap. That would change the prize from a discovery prize to one that also recognises development, and the committee should say so openly. I would not make that change on the strength of a contested priority claim that none of us can verify from the files. Mojsov's synthesis and characterisation of the active form is the step that explains the pharmacology. I therefore keep the discovery trio and treat a Knudsen-for-Mojsov substitution as a fallback, not a preference. I also prefer her suggestion of a different year over squeezing a fourth name into this one.

responses.point: Rickard Sandberg calls Mojsov's place the weakest link in the trio but keeps her. He also thinks a two-part prize is not worth the dilution of the credited names, and notes that long-term safety and durability of the obesity benefit are still being characterised.
responses.response: I share his judgement on a second part. The GLP-1 part already uses all three names, and a second part would add a different story that I do not think improves the citation. On Mojsov we differ in degree. I do not call her the weakest link, because I think the case for the active form is mechanistically specific, but I accept that her priority is the point most open to challenge, so the committee should test it explicitly. On durability, I think the weight-regain and long-term safety questions concern how the drugs are used and do not alter the discovery. Large independent trials have already established the effect on glycaemia, weight and cardiorenal outcomes, so I do not count them against maturity.

responses.point: Thomas Perlmann notes that Habener and Bell, who are not on the supplied credit list, did early work on the proglucagon-derived peptides, so any three-person configuration looks incomplete. He also asks whether a second part, CAR-T or TOR, would be better than a single prize.
responses.response: I accept that the early proglucagon work is a real gap, and my round-1 treatment of attribution as unresolved was too light on it. Earlier cloning and sequencing of the proglucagon-derived peptides established the precursor, while the step that matters for the prize is the active truncated form and its insulinotropic action. That is why I think the omission affects the wording of the citation more than the three names. I would keep the citation on the physiology and active form, not on the precursor. On a second part I take a different view from his listing of TOR as an alternative. Hall's yeast genetics is decisive, but the clinical translation beyond transplantation and a few cancers is narrow. I would sooner give B033 alone than build a pairing that dilutes it.

responses.point: Per Svenningsson, as chair, asks whether CAR-T could be paired with GLP-1 as a second part without breaking the three-person cap, since the GLP-1 part already uses three names. He also asks whether translational impact for the unfolded protein response is mature enough to be a real alternative.
responses.response: The three-person cap makes that pairing costly, because the cap applies across the whole configuration. A CAR-T part would require dropping a GLP-1 name or accepting a very thin second part, and I do not think either is justified. A CAR-T pair with June and Sadelain would leave Rosenberg's clinical precedent outside the prize and Eshhar outside the credited list. Both issues are visible in my own round-1 comments. For the unfolded protein response I agree with his doubt. Walter and Mori are a clean pair and the cell biology is outstanding, but the medical consequence is still indirect, so it does not displace B001 as my third choice. On B039 I keep it as my first alternative, not as a part to add this year.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 form can be defended against the earlier proglucagon work (Habener, Bell), which I cannot verify from the supplied files.
Whether the committee wants a prize that reaches the drugs, which would put Knudsen's claim ahead of Mojsov's.
Whether CAR-T can be fairly configured given Eshhar's absence and the Rosenberg question; this matters if the committee reopens a second part.
Whether the weight-regain and long-term safety data change the maturity assessment; I judge that they do not.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My documented ties are to Sten Grillner, Patrik Ernfors and Thomas Perlmann (a 2009 co-authored paper on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons), and none of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot. I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, or to anyone credited on B039 or B001. Motor-circuit neuroscience is closest to B018, which is not in my configuration. I see no need for recusal.
